newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco allows banks to cross-trade currencies.
newsitem.headline: Morocco allows banks to cross-trade currencies.

text.p: Morocco, aiming to speed liberalisation of the foreign exchange market, will allow domestic banks to start exchanging hard currencies with foreign financial institutions, the central bank said.

In a circular received by Reuters on Wednesday, Bank al-Maghrib said legally established banks: "Are authorised to start purchase and sale of foreign currency (cross rate) operations with Bank al-Maghrib and foreign banks."
The circular was issued on January 27, 1997.
It said the interest rate applied to these operations "is freely negotiated between the two parties". It also lifted a commission previously imposed by the Office des Changes regulatory bureau.

"The monetary authorities move is a good thing for us and for our clients...It is an important step towards the total liberalisation of Morocco's forex market," a dealer at a Casablanca-based bank told Reuters.
"It will stimulate the market and help small and medium sized enterprises to collect funds more easily than in the past for import/export operations," he added.
The Office des Changes earlier issued another circular on the change saying "the cross rate operations should not be translated by borrowings or overdrafts with foreign banks."

The central bank circular said the cross-rate liberalisation covers all traded foreign currencies on the Moroccan market -- about 25 currencies according to one banker -- but not those of the Arab Maghreb Union which comprises Algeria, Libya, Mauritania, Morocco and Tunisia.
The central bank circular said banks must report daily when transactions exceed the equivalent of five million dirhams ($0.5 million). This must be done by 6 p.m. (1800 GMT) at the latest.
It also fixed the equivalent of 2.0 million dirhams as "minimum deposit" of domestic banks at Bank al-Maghrib.

"The gradual liberalisation of the forex market will help banks to get more experience and avoid professional accidents...", Mouna Lahlou, an analyst at Casablanca Finance Intermediation, said. The long-term aim is total convertibility of the Moroccan dirham, which is widely considered a stable currency. ($=9.16 dirhams)
